lessonTitle: Mycobacteria and Atypical Bacteria: Tuberculosis, Intracellular Pathogens and Spirochaetes

blocks.text: A 45-year-old man has had six weeks of cough, drenching night sweats and weight loss. His sputum smear, stained with hot carbol fuchsin, shows slender red rods against a blue background, while an ordinary Gram stain of the same sputum showed almost nothing. The organism's waxy wall explains both the odd staining and the slow, tenacious disease it causes.

blocks.markdown: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* is a slow-growing, obligately aerobic bacillus. Its cell wall is rich in **mycolic acids**, long-chain waxy lipids, which make it hydrophobic, resistant to drying, many disinfectants and many antibiotics, and unable to take up the Gram stain reliably. Its generation time is about 20 hours, so cultures take weeks. Because it is intracellular within macrophages, protection depends on **cell-mediated immunity**.

blocks.title: Acid-fast bacilli
blocks.text: Acid-fast bacilli retain carbol fuchsin even after decolourisation with acid-alcohol, because the mycolic acid-rich wall binds the dye tightly once heated. In the Ziehl-Neelsen stain mycobacteria appear red against a blue counterstain (methylene blue); non-acid-fast cells and background are decolourised and take up the counterstain.

blocks.title: Why acid-fast staining is chosen
blocks.prompt: A laboratory receives a sputum specimen from a patient with a suspected mycobacterial infection. Explain why a Ziehl-Neelsen stain, rather than only a Gram stain, is requested, and what a positive result looks like.

steps.text: The mycobacterial wall is thick with mycolic acid lipids, so ordinary aqueous dyes in the Gram stain penetrate poorly and the organism stains weakly or not at all.
Heating carbol fuchsin drives dye into the waxy wall. Once taken up, the dye resists removal by acid-alcohol decolouriser, hence 'acid-fast'.
A counterstain colours everything else blue, so positive bacilli are red rods on a blue background.

blocks.answer: Acid-fast staining exploits the mycolic acid wall: mycobacteria are red rods on a blue background, whereas the Gram stain is unreliable for them.

blocks.markdown: **Primary tuberculosis.** Infection is by inhaling **droplet nuclei** from a person with pulmonary disease. Bacilli reach the alveoli, are engulfed by alveolar macrophages and survive by blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion. They multiply, and infected cells carry bacilli to hilar lymph nodes. The initial peripheral lung lesion (Ghon focus) plus involved hilar nodes is the **Ghon complex**. After two to eight weeks, T-helper 1 cells release interferon-gamma, activating macrophages. This produces **granulomas** with epithelioid macrophages, multinucleate giant cells and central **caseating necrosis**. In most immunocompetent people, the granulomas contain the infection, leaving **latent TB**: no symptoms and not infectious, but live bacilli persist.

**Reactivation (post-primary) tuberculosis.** If immunity wanes, for example in HIV infection, malnutrition, diabetes, ageing or treatment with corticosteroids or TNF-alpha inhibitors, dormant bacilli multiply. Disease classically occurs in the **upper lobes** (apical regions), where oxygen tension is high, and tends to cavitate, which makes the patient infectious. Haematogenous spread can produce **miliary tuberculosis** and extrapulmonary disease (lymph nodes, pleura, spine, meninges, kidneys). Immune response damage, not the organism's toxins, causes the tissue destruction.

blocks.title: Why TB culture is slow
blocks.prompt: A bacillus with a generation time of 20 hours starts at 100 cells. How long to reach 10^5 cells, assuming continuous exponential growth?

steps.text: Fold increase = 10^5 / 100 = 1000. Solve 2^n = 1000, so n = log2(1000) = about 10 generations.
Time = n x g = 10 x 20 h = 200 hours, about 8 days.

blocks.answer: About 200 hours (8 days), which explains why mycobacterial culture takes weeks.

blocks.markdown: **Intracellular and other atypical bacteria.** 'Atypical' refers to organisms that do not behave as typical Gram-stained, culturable, beta-lactam-susceptible bacteria. Many live **inside host cells**, which makes antibiotic penetration and immune clearance harder. Key examples: *Legionella pneumophila* (inhaled from contaminated water systems; Legionnaires' disease, a severe pneumonia often with hyponatraemia and diarrhoea); *Chlamydia trachomatis* (obligate intracellular; urethritis, cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, trachoma); *Rickettsia* species (tick- or louse-borne; fever and rash, spotted and typhus fevers); *Coxiella burnetii* (Q fever, from animal products). **Spirochaetes** are thin, spiral bacteria that are poorly seen by Gram stain: *Treponema pallidum* causes syphilis and *Borrelia burgdorferi* causes Lyme disease. *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* has no cell wall, so beta-lactams do not work.

items: Mycolic acid wall: acid-fast, slow growth, tough.
Primary TB: droplet nuclei, macrophage uptake, Ghon complex, granuloma with caseation.
Latent TB: contained by Th1 and interferon-gamma, can reactivate.
Reactivation: apical cavitation when immunity falls.
Atypical pathogens: intracellular or wall-less, so beta-lactams are unreliable.

blocks.title: Immunity both protects and damages
blocks.text: Granuloma formation contains M. tuberculosis but the caseating necrosis and cavitation cause the disease. Failure of cell-mediated immunity, as in advanced HIV infection, is the main trigger for reactivation.

blocks.title: Do not rely on a Gram stain for TB
blocks.text: A negative Gram stain does not exclude mycobacteria or most atypical pathogens. Request acid-fast staining and culture when TB is suspected, and remember that a positive latent test does not mean active disease.

points: Mycolic acid-rich walls make mycobacteria acid-fast, slow-growing and resistant.
Primary TB forms a Ghon complex and caseating granulomas; most infections become latent.
Reactivation occurs when cell-mediated immunity falls, typically with apical cavitation.
Legionella, Chlamydia trachomatis, Rickettsia and Coxiella are intracellular pathogens; spirochaetes cause syphilis and Lyme disease.

questions.stem: Which cell wall component makes Mycobacterium tuberculosis acid-fast?

distractorRationale.b: LPS is the outer membrane component of Gram-negative bacteria.
distractorRationale.c: Teichoic acids are in Gram-positive walls.
distractorRationale.d: Capsules are not what makes mycobacteria acid-fast.

questions.explanation: Mycolic acids are long waxy lipids that bind carbol fuchsin when heated and resist acid-alcohol decolourisation. This is the basis of acid-fast staining.

questions.stem: On a Ziehl-Neelsen stained smear, how do mycobacteria appear?

options.text: Red rods on a blue background
Blue rods on a red background

questions.correctOptionText: Red rods on a blue background

distractorRationale.c: Purple cocci in clusters describe Gram-positive staphylococci.
distractorRationale.d: Pink diplococci describe Gram-negative Neisseria on Gram stain.

questions.explanation: The waxy wall retains carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol, so mycobacteria are red. Other material is decolourised and takes up the blue methylene blue counterstain.

questions.stem: Which histological finding is characteristic of the host response in tuberculosis?

options.text: Granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, giant cells and caseating necrosis
Sheets of neutrophils with abscess formation only
Pseudomembrane of fibrin and neutrophils on the mucosa

questions.correctOptionText: Granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, giant cells and caseating necrosis

distractorRationale.b: Pyogenic abscesses are typical of other pyogenic bacteria.
distractorRationale.c: Pseudomembranes are seen in C. difficile colitis and diphtheria.
distractorRationale.d: Eosinophilic infiltrates are typical of allergic and helminth responses.

questions.explanation: Th1 cells and interferon-gamma activate macrophages to form granulomas around the bacilli, with central caseating necrosis. This contains the infection but also causes tissue damage.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who has had no TB symptoms for decades, and had a positive latent TB test years ago, starts high-dose corticosteroids for another illness and develops cough and upper-lobe cavitation. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Reactivation of latent infection because impaired cell-mediated immunity no longer contains the bacilli
Primary infection acquired from the corticosteroid preparation
Endotoxin release from the dormant bacilli

questions.correctOptionText: Reactivation of latent infection because impaired cell-mediated immunity no longer contains the bacilli

distractorRationale.b: The corticosteroids do not transmit TB; she had prior infection.
distractorRationale.c: Mycobacteria do not have LPS endotoxin.
distractorRationale.d: Tissue damage in TB is largely immune-mediated, not toxin-mediated.

questions.explanation: Granulomas depend on T cells and macrophage activation, which corticosteroids suppress. Dormant bacilli then multiply, usually in the oxygen-rich upper lobes, and cavitate.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man who works maintaining the water cooling tower of a large hotel develops fever, confusion, diarrhoea and lobar pneumonia, with a low serum sodium. Which organism is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: water systems, pneumonia with extrapulmonary features and hyponatraemia.
distractorRationale.c: C. trachomatis causes genital and ocular disease.
distractorRationale.d: TB causes a chronic illness, not an acute water-borne pneumonia.

questions.explanation: Legionella is an intracellular organism that grows in warm water systems and is inhaled in aerosols. It causes Legionnaires' pneumonia, frequently with diarrhoea, confusion and hyponatraemia.

questions.stem: In a study of 200 patients with culture-confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, a Ziehl-Neelsen sputum smear was positive in 130. Calculate the sensitivity of the smear compared with culture, as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all culture-confirmed cases: 130 / 200 = 0.65 or 65%. A negative smear therefore does not exclude TB, so culture is still required.

questions.stem: Mycobacterium tuberculosis has a generation time of about 20 hours. Starting from 1 000 cells, calculate the time in hours needed to reach 1.6 x 10^7 cells assuming continuous exponential growth.
questions.explanation: The fold increase is 1.6 x 10^7 / 10^3 = 1.6 x 10^4, so the number of generations is log2(16 000) which is about 13.97, roughly 14. Time = 14 x 20 h = 280 hours, which shows why mycobacterial culture takes weeks.

questions.stem: Describe the pathogenesis of primary tuberculosis from inhalation to the formation of latent infection, and state three circumstances in which latent infection may reactivate.
markingGuide: Inhalation of droplet nuclei; bacilli reach alveoli and are engulfed by macrophages, surviving by preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion
Spread to hilar lymph nodes; Ghon focus and Ghon complex
Th1 response and interferon-gamma activate macrophages
Granuloma with caseating necrosis contains infection, giving latent TB
Reactivation with immunosuppression, for example HIV, corticosteroids or TNF-alpha inhibitors, malnutrition, diabetes or ageing
questions.explanation: Primary disease is controlled by cell-mediated immunity forming granulomas. Any process that weakens that immunity allows dormant bacilli to re-emerge.

questions.stem: Explain why acid-fast staining, rather than the Gram stain, is used to detect mycobacteria, and outline the key steps of the Ziehl-Neelsen method.
markingGuide: Wall is rich in mycolic acids (waxy, hydrophobic) so Gram dyes penetrate poorly
Carbol fuchsin applied with heat to enter the wall
Decolourisation with acid-alcohol does not remove dye from mycobacteria (acid-fast)
Methylene blue counterstain colours other cells blue
Result: red bacilli on a blue background
questions.explanation: The key is the wall lipid. It both blocks the Gram stain and retains the carbol fuchsin, which is why a special stain is needed.

questions.stem: Name two intracellular bacterial pathogens, the syndrome each causes and one reason why intracellular location complicates treatment or immune clearance.
markingGuide: First pathogen with correct syndrome (such as Legionella pneumophila: Legionnaires' pneumonia; Chlamydia trachomatis: urethritis, cervicitis or trachoma; Rickettsia: spotted fever; Coxiella: Q fever; M. tuberculosis: tuberculosis)
Intracellular bacteria are protected from antibody and many antibiotics that penetrate cells poorly
Clearance requires cell-mediated immunity, such as T cells and activated macrophages
Treatment may need drugs that accumulate in cells, such as macrolides or tetracyclines
questions.explanation: Intracellular organisms hide from antibodies and are poorly reached by some drugs. Naming correct organism-syndrome pairs demonstrates the clinical link.
